To say the numbers from 100 to a million: o sută douăzeci, două mii cinci sute.
To use "de" after large numbers: douăzeci de lei, o sută de ani.

To tell the history of a city briefly.
On Saturday morning, Mrs Pop, Nora, Radu and Mițu (in a basket) walk into the café "Ceasul". Mr Grigore is surprised: Mrs Pop hasn't set foot here for ten years. Radu is holding the blue notebook.
Elisabeta…? I can't believe it. How long since you were last here? Ten years?
Ten years, nine months and a few days. But who's counting… Grigore, I've brought you something. From Vasile.
Grandpa wrote a notebook about the clock. Look at page forty-two.
"The secret of the clock"… A little wheel made by Iosif Kovács in 1952. Iosif! He was my teacher! I worked in his workshop for thirteen years, from 1968 to 1981.
Then you know what it's about?
A quarter of a turn… Good Lord. I tightened it all the way. For ten years I've been tightening it, every month, tighter and tighter. I thought that was how it had to be.
Grigore, Vasile didn't have time to tell you. It's not your fault.
Give me three minutes. And a small screwdriver. Radu, bring me that lamp from the shelf.
A quarter to ten. Saturday, 14 November.
Done. I've loosened it a quarter of a turn. Now… let's see. Elisabeta, would you like to start the clock? It would be right.
It's going. After ten years, it's going.
"nu-mi vine să cred" = I can't believe it
"despre ce e vorba" = what it is about
"n-a apucat să" = didn't have time to
Years are read as whole numbers: 1890 = o mie opt sute nouăzeci; 2026 = două mii douăzeci și șase.
It is read "secolul al șaisprezecelea". Roman numerals are very common for centuries.
Careful: in speech, 14 is said "paișpe" and 16 "șaișpe". In writing and careful speech: paisprezece, șaisprezece.
"Sută" and "mie" are feminine: o sută, două sute, o mie, două mii. "Milion" is neuter: un milion, două milioane.
In Romanian, thousands are separated with a full stop and decimals with a comma: 1.500 (one thousand five hundred); 2,5 (two point five).
When a number ends in 20–99 (or is 100, 1000 etc.), "de" appears between the number and the noun. From 1 to 19 there is no "de".
Only the last two digits matter: 105 lei (no "de"), but 120 de lei (with "de").
The date is said with cardinal numbers (one, two, three…), not ordinals, except for the first day.
On the first of December it is Romania's National Day.
Use "pe" for the day ("pe 3 mai") and "în" for the year or month ("în 1993", "în mai").
Centuries are usually written with Roman numerals. They are read with an ordinal number: "al" + number + "-lea".
From 20 upwards, cardinal numbers are often used in speech: "secolul douăzeci" (less often "al douăzecilea").
For history you use the compound perfect and the simple passive: "a fost construit", "a fost fondată".
The church was built in the 14th century.
Matthias Corvinus was born in Cluj in 1443.
"A fost + participle" is the passive. The participle agrees with the subject: zidul a fost construit, biserica a fost construită, casele au fost construite.
On the first of December it is the National Day.
I loosened it a quarter of a turn.
I don't like baskets. A tomcat with dignity does not sit in a basket. But on Saturday morning I made an exception, because Mrs Pop said it was a historic day. And she was right.

The café "Ceasul" is on Matei Corvin Street, at number 12, in an old 18th-century house. On the walls there are fifty-three clocks. I had time to count them, because in the basket I had nothing else to do.

Some clocks are small, the size of a plate. Others are big, the size of a wardrobe. One has an owl that comes out every hour. Another has a sailor who dances. But the most beautiful is the pendulum clock by the door: two metres tall, made of walnut, with a white dial and Roman numerals.
When Mrs Pop came in, Mr Grigore dropped a cup. The cup broke into a hundred pieces. Nobody looked at it.

You know the rest. The notebook, page forty-two, Iosif's little wheel, a quarter of a turn. Mr Grigore worked for three minutes, with a lamp and a small screwdriver. His hands, which usually shake when he pours the coffee, were perfectly steady.
Then Mrs Pop put her hand on the pendulum and gave it a little push. And the clock began to go.

Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock. A deep, slow sound, like the heart of a big sleeping animal. The whole café fell silent. The two students at the corner table put down their phones. A lady in a green hat put her hand to her mouth.
Mr Grigore took an old pocket watch out of his pocket, opened it and set the hands of the clock. Five past ten. "Now it's exact," he said. His voice was trembling a little.

Then something happened that I had never seen. Mr Grigore came out from behind the counter, went up to Mrs Pop and hugged her. Two old people, in the middle of a café, with fifty-three clocks around them.
"Did you know?" he asked her quietly. "About ten past four?"
"I knew," she said. "I knew all along."

Nora was crying and laughing at the same time, as people do when they are happy and sad at once. Radu took his violin out of its case, because Radu always has his violin with him, and began to play an old song softly. Mrs Pop recognised it from the first note: it was the song Vasile used to play on the shepherd's flute, on the rock at Turda Gorge, fifty years ago.

At eleven o'clock sharp, the clock struck. Eleven long, deep strokes. And at the same moment, as if at a signal, the other fifty-two clocks struck too. The owl came out. The sailor danced. It was the loudest noise I have ever heard in my life.

I jumped out of the basket and hid under a table. Everyone laughed. Mr Grigore brought me a little saucer of whipped cream, "for the hero of the day". I don't understand why I am the hero. But the cream was very good, and I never argue with cream.

Reading text: The history of Cluj
Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. Tap any word to see what it means. At the end there are 4 questions.
In the 2nd century, the Romans built a settlement here called Napoca.
In the Middle Ages, the city was called Klausenburg in German and Kolozsvár in Hungarian.
In 1405, Cluj became a free royal town. It had thick walls and more than twenty towers.
In 1443, Matthias Corvinus, one of the greatest kings of Hungary, was born here. The house where he was born still exists today.
In the 19th century, Cluj became an important cultural centre. The university was founded in 1872.
In 1918, Transylvania united with Romania. In 1974, the city got the name Cluj-Napoca.
Today Cluj has about three hundred thousand inhabitants and over one hundred thousand students.
